newsitem.title: JORDAN: British jet car turns up speed in Jordanian desert.
newsitem.headline: British jet car turns up speed in Jordanian desert.

text.p: Britain's jet-powered Thrust car thundered across the deserts of south Jordan on Tuesday, gearing up for its twin assault on the world land speed record and the sound barrier.
Bedouin camel herders looked on with binoculars as the 10-tonne car tore across the mud-flats of Al-Jafr at close to 500 miles per hour (800 kph), churning up billowing clouds of dust.
"I want to see the car go above 600 miles per hour (960 kph) in Jordan and with a bit of luck we might be up to that speed tomorrow," said project leader Richard Noble after the early morning run.
Noble, heading the Thrust challenge on his own land speed record of 633.47 mph (1,019.44 kph), said the team were aiming for a world record run in the United States in September.

British Royal Air Force pilot Andy Green would then turn up the power from car's jet engines, taken from a Phantom warplane, and bid to become the first man on four wheels to break the speed of sound (about 750 mph/1,200 kph).
Shortly after dawn on Tuesday a radio car with flashing lights and sirens cleared camels and herders from the area.
The 16.5 metre (54 feet) Thrust car then raced down the 10 mile (16 km) desert strip before being dragged to a halt by a single parachute.
The Thrust team say they will not attempt to break the world record in al-Jafr, a stretch of bone-dry mudflats about 125 miles (200 km) south of Amman, because it is not big enough.

To notch up a world record the car's speed must be measured over the same one mile (1.6 km) track on two separate runs, in opposite directions. The car, even with powerful brakes and the parachute, needs about seven miles to slow down.
"When you're using up a kilometre every two or three seconds the desert runs out very quickly (so) it's unlikely we'd be able to safely break a record here," Green said after his run.
"We will hopefully get up to the same speed as the record, 633 mph. If we get up there we can prove the car will break the record as soon as we get to America," he added.
Green said the team had overcome problems with the rear steering of the car's solid aluminium wheels and would use the remaining tests in Jordan to see how the car reacted to extreme speed.
"At about 600 mph we start to...form shockwaves around the car. It's very important to understand those shockwaves when we try ultimately to take the car supersonic," he said.

Noble brought his team to Jordan for tests last year but finally gave in when the heaviest rains in five years turned the al-Jafr track, mapped out on the same desert where scenes from Lawrence of Arabia were filmed, into a lake.

He is racing to claim the record before U.S. driver Craig Breedlove, who had to postpone his own challenge last year when his car, the Spirit of America, was damaged in a high speed accident in the Black Rock desert of Nevada.
